columns_synthesis.headline: All three run different platforms (ServiceNow at a $40B/2M-ticket enterprise, BMC Helix at ~2,200 employees, Freshservice at ~450), but the story of why they moved is nearly identical: a legacy tool that would not scale, no reliable CMDB or asset inventory, and compliance pressure (GxP or SOC 2) that turned IT housekeeping into a leadership-sponsored project.

canonical_quote.quote: It started as an IT-driven project, honestly. I inherited the legacy tool and it was falling apart - outages, tickets getting lost. Once I built the business case around compliance risk, it got elevated, and our VP of IT and our Head of Quality co-sponsored it.

agreements.statement: The initiative began inside IT and only became strategic/leadership-visible once compliance risk was attached to it.

positions.gist: Started as site- and division-level complaints about slowness, then escalated to a global strategic IT initiative.

citation.quote: So, it started at the site level, grew into a strategic IT initiative, and then was implemented globally.

positions.gist: IT-driven until a compliance-risk business case got VP of IT and Head of Quality to co-sponsor.

citation.quote: So it became bigger than just an IT refresh, but it wasn't part of some grand ERP-style transformation program.

positions.gist: IT and security-driven at first; the SOC 2 requirement from the CFO's office is what earned leadership attention.

citation.quote: Mostly IT and security-driven at first. It became more strategic once the SOC 2 requirement came from our CFO's office - that got leadership attention pretty fast.

agreements.statement: Absence of a real CMDB / asset inventory in the legacy environment was a named driver for the new platform.

positions.gist: Needed centralized management of all IT assets alongside SLA and MTTR improvement.

citation.quote: We also needed centralized management of all IT assets.

positions.gist: ManageEngine had no real CMDB, so no trustworthy inventory of lab equipment or IT hardware.

citation.quote: it didn't have a real CMDB, so we had no reliable asset inventory for our lab equipment or IT hardware

positions.gist: Leadership wanted metrics including how many devices are deployed in the field.

citation.quote: how many devices we have deployed in the field, that kind of thing

agreements.statement: A GxP flag on the change record that routes the change to Quality for review/approval is the concrete compliance capability that justified the platform.

positions.gist: Checking a GxP box on a change triggers specific routing and change workflows Zendesk did not have.

citation.quote: when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have.

positions.gist: GxP tag routes the change through Quality for review and e-signature before implementation, with a full audit trail.

citation.quote: When someone opens a change, they tag whether it's GxP-impacting, and that routes it through Quality for review and electronic signature before it can move to implementation.

conflicts.statement: Whether simplifying to a lightweight tool at small scale is a defensible trade: expert-1 says his company's move off ServiceNow to a Teams-based custom tool cost them asset management and does not scale, while expert-3 reports being deliberately content on a lightweight cloud tool at similar scale.

positions.gist: Judges the small-company simplification decision poorly thought through, with loss of asset management as the repercussion.

citation.quote: I don’t think the decision was well thought through and it doesn’t scale, but for the company size at that time, I guess it made sense to simplify the user experience.

positions.gist: Runs a small org on Freshservice with asset management on and treats it as fit for purpose.

citation.quote: We use Incident, Service Request, Change, Problem, Asset Management, and we recently turned on the Project module for some larger infrastructure rollouts.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-1's small-company tool is a custom Teams/AI build with no asset management at all; expert-3 chose a commercial ITSM suite that includes asset management with a discovery agent.

outliers.gist: Only interviewee speaking from two environments at once - a 2M-ticket, 2,000-site ServiceNow enterprise and a current small company that moved off ServiceNow to a custom AI tool he inherited and dislikes.

citation.quote: Not my decision; it predated me and we have to live with it. One repercussion is we don’t really have asset management for all our IT assets, which is a big pain point for me right now.

notable: The ticket-per-employee ratios are strikingly close despite the scale gap: expert-2 at ~60,000 tickets / ~2,200 employees and expert-3 at ~18,000 / ~450 - roughly 27-40 tickets per employee per year - making expert-1's 2M tickets the only figure without a headcount denominator.
expert-1 is the only one describing modules beyond core ITSM (HR service delivery, Major Incident Management, and a GRC rollout for logging and prioritizing risks such as an overdue pen test).

Both regulated-industry interviewees say change was previously tracked informally: expert-2 states 'changes were tracked in email half the time', and expert-1 notes some of the pre-ServiceNow tooling 'was even paper-based'.

expert-3 is the only one with a non-employee user population - rotating field contractors submitting via email-to-ticket - which shapes his later emphasis on ease of use for a non-technical workforce.
Only expert-2 flags a capability bought but not yet enabled ('We don't have the full AIOps suite turned on yet'), a reminder that module lists overstate live usage.
gaps: Nobody was asked directly about current platform spend in this section, so the scale comparison has volumes and headcounts but no cost baseline.
expert-3 gives no detail on which legacy tool preceded Freshservice, so his migration starting point is not comparable to expert-1's Zendesk or expert-2's ManageEngine.
Only expert-1 and expert-2 discuss GxP-specific workflow requirements; expert-3's compliance driver is SOC 2, so the pharma-specific conclusions rest on two accounts.

columns_synthesis.headline: Company size decides the ranking. The enterprise buyer put scalability and integration first and accepted ServiceNow's premium; both mid-market buyers put total cost of ownership first and ruled ServiceNow out early - one calling roughly triple the BMC quote 'not defensible internally'. All three name nearly the same five criteria and only reorder them.

canonical_quote.quote: ServiceNow was excellent but it was almost triple our BMC quote for a comparable module set, and for our size, that wasn't defensible internally.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow's capability was not in doubt; it was priced out relative to the buyer's size.

positions.gist: Rated ServiceNow excellent but roughly triple the BMC quote for comparable modules.

citation.quote: Honestly, it came down to price relative to capability.

positions.gist: Eliminated ServiceNow quickly on cost as more platform than needed.

citation.quote: We ruled out ServiceNow pretty quickly on cost; it felt like way more platform than we needed at our size.

positions.gist: Acknowledges ServiceNow was the higher-cost option but says integration, scalability and customization outweighed it at enterprise scale.

citation.quote: They weren’t as strong on cost—they were a bit higher—but integration, scalability, and customization tipped the scale.

agreements.statement: Jira Service Management was considered and eliminated by both who looked at it, for the same reason - insufficient depth for CMDB/compliance and enterprise workflow.

positions.gist: Jira lacked needed modules and raised performance concerns at 1-2M tickets; strong for agile, not for major incident and change management.

citation.quote: At the time, Jira wasn’t scalable enough and lacked modules we needed.

positions.gist: Ruled Jira out early for lacking CMDB and compliance workflow depth.

citation.quote: We also briefly looked at Jira Service Management but ruled it out pretty early - it just didn't have the depth we needed for CMDB and compliance workflows.

agreements.statement: Integration with the existing HR/identity stack is a top-five criterion for all three, though the named systems differ by scale (Workday/IAM, SAP and Workday, Azure AD and Intune).

positions.gist: Ranks integration capabilities first among the top five and rates ServiceNow 9/10 on it.

citation.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems.

positions.gist: Places integration capability fourth, specifically SAP and Workday.

citation.quote: integration with our existing systems like SAP and Workday

positions.gist: Places integration fifth, scoped tightly to Azure AD and Intune.

citation.quote: Fifth, integration with Azure AD and Intune.

agreements.statement: Zendesk is treated as a customer-support tool that falls short for internal IT, by the two who evaluated it.

positions.gist: Intuitive for customer service and small/mid-market, but lacking advanced workflow automation and customization.

citation.quote: Zendesk is very intuitive for customer service and fits small to mid-market needs, but it lacks advanced workflow automation and customization.

positions.gist: Felt built for customer support rather than internal IT, with weak asset management.

citation.quote: Zendesk felt built more for customer support than internal IT - the asset management piece was weak.

conflicts.statement: Freshservice's fitness as a chosen platform: expert-3 selected it as the sweet spot, while expert-2 pushed it down his list fast despite it being the cheapest quote.

positions.gist: Picked Freshservice for modern interface, built-in asset management with discovery agent, and price.

citation.quote: Freshservice hit the sweet spot: modern interface, built-in asset management with a discovery agent, and a price point that made sense for us.

positions.gist: Cheapest of the four but the compliance workflow story was too thin to keep it in contention.

citation.quote: Freshservice was cheapest but their compliance workflow story was thinner, so it dropped down our list fast.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-2 needed GxP-grade change-approval workflows out of the box; expert-3's compliance need was SOC 2 audit trail, so the depth gap was not disqualifying.

conflicts.statement: Whether Ivanti is a credible finalist: expert-2 ranked it close enough to be BMC's runner-up, while expert-3 discounted it based on hands-on experience of clunky administration.

positions.gist: Ivanti was close to BMC on price and offered a three-year lock, losing only on custom configuration needed for GxP.

citation.quote: Ivanti was close in price to BMC, but their compliance and change-approval workflows needed more custom configuration to meet our GxP requirements.

positions.gist: Prior operating experience with Ivanti was negative - clunky admin, slow to configure.

citation.quote: Ivanti I already knew from my last job, and honestly it wasn't a great memory - clunky admin, slow to configure.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-2 assessed Ivanti through a sales evaluation; expert-3 had lived with it as an administrator, which is where his objection sits.

outliers.gist: The only buyer who ranks scalability first and treats cost as a tolerable trade-off, and the only one describing a formal POC-and-approval chain up to VP/CIO.

citation.quote: So scalability was the top criterion—working with a Fortune 500 company at roughly $40B revenue and 2,000 sites—this was critical.

notable: Two independent price signals point the same way: expert-1 indexes ServiceNow at ~$100/user/month against Zendesk at $50-55 and Jira at $20-21, and expert-2 says ServiceNow came in at almost triple his BMC quote.

expert-1's own scores undercut a pure-capability case: he rates ServiceNow 6 on TCO and 7 on user experience - below Jira, Zendesk and BMC at 8 - while giving it 9 on integration and 9 on customization.

expert-2 is the only one describing a pricing-diligence tactic: multi-year quotes rather than year-one pricing because of stories about year-two and three increases, with ServiceNow transparent about escalation and Ivanti and BMC offering multi-year locks.
expert-1 names an unusual evaluation discipline - demo first, then a short POC in the vendor's environment to prove a specific claim such as Workday onboarding flowing into ServiceNow.

Both mid-market buyers price administration burden into the decision: expert-2 because he has only three people supporting the platform, expert-3 because his users are a non-technical field workforce.
expert-2 cites BMC's pre-built pharma and med device content as the tiebreaker - vertical templates, not raw platform strength, decided that deal.
gaps: Only expert-1 provides comparative per-user pricing; the others give relative multiples, so no like-for-like cost table can be built.
Only expert-1 describes the approval chain (director/senior director building the case, VP approval, CIO for larger spend); we do not know who signed at the other two organizations.
BMC was formally evaluated only by expert-1 and expert-2, and Freshservice only by expert-2 and expert-3, so no vendor here has all three assessments.
None was asked whether they revisited the decision after go-live, so we cannot tell whether the criteria ranking held up in hindsight.

columns_synthesis.headline: The scoring is consistent in shape and inverted in preference: everyone puts ServiceNow highest on raw capability and integration and lowest on TCO and ease of administration, and the lighter tools the reverse. Each then rates their own platform highest 'for us specifically' - and each names the structural cost of that choice, from ServiceNow's admin overhead to BMC's thin partner pool to Freshservice's clunky automation builder.

canonical_quote.quote: ServiceNow is probably a 9 in raw capability, but you have to build a lot of it yourself.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow leads on integration breadth and raw capability but is scored down for complexity and cost - the same trade named from three different platforms.

positions.gist: Cheaper competitors lack ServiceNow's capability and flexibility; ServiceNow needs dedicated admins and partners.

citation.quote: Obviously, cost is number one—many competitors are lower cost. But they typically don't have as much capability and flexibility as ServiceNow.

positions.gist: Scores ServiceNow 9 on integration and 9 on raw capability but 5 on TCO and 6 on ease of administration for a small team.

citation.quote: ServiceNow is powerful but complex, I'd put it at a 6 for a team our size.

positions.gist: Scores ServiceNow 9 on integration and 9 on asset management on paper, but 6 on ease of use and 4 on TCO.

citation.quote: ServiceNow's probably the strongest on paper, I'd give it a 9, but it's overkill for us.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow's advantage is partly ecosystem scale - more connectors, more integrators, a bigger community - not only product features.

positions.gist: BMC's smaller partner pool made specialized integrations slower to staff than ServiceNow's would have been.

citation.quote: When we needed a specialized integration, our BMC partner pool was smaller, and it sometimes took longer to find someone who'd done exactly what we needed. With ServiceNow, there's just a much bigger community and more integrators to choose from.

positions.gist: Relies on partners for advanced configuration and upgrades on top of dedicated internal admins.

citation.quote: You need dedicated admins, and partners for more advanced configurations and integrations.

agreements.statement: Each acknowledges a real limitation in the platform they run rather than defending it outright.

positions.gist: Concedes ServiceNow needs more maintenance than competitors and consumed 3-5 people at 30-40% of their time.

citation.quote: There’s definitely maintenance and upkeep—probably more than other competitors because it can be a very complex system.

positions.gist: Concedes BMC's partner ecosystem is thin when specialized integration work is needed.

citation.quote: Yes, that's fair. When we needed a specialized integration, our BMC partner pool was smaller

positions.gist: Concedes Freshservice's automation builder gets clunky under chained conditional logic as approval chains grow.

citation.quote: It's not a hard wall, but you notice the automation builder gets clunky once you're chaining a lot of conditional logic.

conflicts.statement: Ivanti's standing: expert-2 rates it mid-pack and calls it BMC's closest runner-up, while expert-3 rates it lowest of four on ease of use (5) and 6 on integration from hands-on experience - though he allows its asset piece was decent.

positions.gist: Ivanti close to BMC on cost and general ITSM function; 7s across integration, TCO and ease of administration.

citation.quote: Probably Ivanti. They're close on cost and on general ITSM functionality.

positions.gist: Rates Ivanti worst on ease of use and weak on integration due to manual config, while allowing its asset management was decent.

citation.quote: Ivanti was a 6 in my experience, lots of manual config.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-2's view comes from a sales-cycle evaluation, expert-3's from having administered Ivanti at a previous employer.

outliers.gist: The only one who assesses vendors on corporate trajectory - CEO performance, market cap growth, the Moveworks acquisition, a move toward CRM - rather than feature scores.

citation.quote: I admire that they're leaning headfirst into AI—now they have agents, and with the Moveworks acquisition as well.

notable: The two numeric TCO ratings for ServiceNow agree it is worst of its peer set: expert-2 gives it 5 and expert-3 gives it 4, while both give their own platform 8-9.
expert-1 is the only one to quantify ServiceNow's run cost - 3-5 employees at roughly 30-40% of their time each, plus partners for upgrades - and concedes it dented ROI 'slightly'.
expert-3 offers the sharpest time-to-value contrast: live in about ten weeks versus a belief that ServiceNow would not have been live in under six months and would have cost multiples.
expert-2's stated differentiator for BMC is not technical - out-of-the-box compliance templates plus an account team that understood GxP language without explanation.
expert-1 credits Zendesk's simplicity as a genuine competitive advantage and says Jira's AI push makes it 'quite competitive' - notable from the interviewee who ruled both out.
expert-1 reports that AI posture, not core ITSM function, drove the small-company move away from ServiceNow: at the time it 'weren’t leaning into it as heavily' while the chosen vendor was AI-first.
gaps: No vendor is scored by all three: BMC by expert-1 and expert-2, Freshservice by expert-2 and expert-3, Zendesk by expert-1 and expert-3, so every head-to-head rests on at most two ratings.
expert-1 gives narrative rather than numeric scores in this section, so his comparisons cannot be placed on the same scale as the others'.
Only expert-1 was asked about vendor strategic direction and AI roadmap; the others say nothing about AI, so nothing can be concluded about how mid-market buyers weigh it.
Only expert-1 quantifies ongoing admin headcount; the others rate ease of administration but give no staffing numbers.

columns_synthesis.headline: Time to live tracks platform weight almost linearly - about ten weeks on Freshservice, seven months on BMC Helix, nine to twelve on ServiceNow - and in every case the hard part was not the platform. Native connectors handled the HR/identity system cleanly for all three, while the second, more customized system needed hand-built API or scripting work that was not in the original plan.

canonical_quote.quote: Workday integration was fairly smooth - BMC had a solid connector for HR data sync, onboarding and offboarding trigger workflows. SAP was harder.

agreements.statement: Out-of-the-box connectors covered the standard identity/HR integration; anything touching a customized or legacy back-end system needed custom API or scripting work.

positions.gist: Out-of-the-box APIs existed but a middle layer and a custom API were needed to reach legacy ERP data feeding Databricks.

citation.quote: They had some out-of-the-box APIs, but we had legacy systems and tools that those APIs wouldn’t connect to, so we built a middle layer to make them talk.

positions.gist: Workday ran on BMC's native connector; the customized SAP inventory side required a custom REST API built in-house.

citation.quote: For SAP it was custom REST API work built by our integration engineer, because our SAP instance is fairly customized on the inventory side.

positions.gist: Azure AD sync was native and took a day; Intune device data needed native integration plus manual scripting for custom field mapping.

citation.quote: Intune was a bit more work - we wanted device data flowing into the asset CMDB, and we ended up using a combination of the native integration plus some manual scripting to get certain custom fields to map correctly.

agreements.statement: Effort was underestimated in the original plan, and the overrun landed on internal staff rather than the vendor.

positions.gist: Expected 6-7 months, took 9-12; user testing was undefined so unprepared internal resources had to be pulled in.

citation.quote: we expected a 6-7 month implementation, and it ended up taking 9-12 months—roughly another quarter we had to absorb

positions.gist: The SAP custom integration consumed six or seven weeks that had not been budgeted.

citation.quote: That took an extra six or seven weeks we hadn't originally budgeted.

agreements.statement: End-user adoption, not technical configuration, was the dominant implementation challenge for the two mid-market implementers, and both responded with hands-on enablement.

positions.gist: Site staff resisted the new portal; lunch-and-learns and walkthrough videos, and about two months before channels stabilized.

citation.quote: It took about two months post-go-live before ticket volume through the correct channels stabilized.

positions.gist: The challenge was field staff texting or calling him directly instead of raising tickets, requiring a change management push and incentives.

citation.quote: The biggest challenge honestly wasn't the platform - it was getting field staff to actually use tickets instead of texting or calling me directly.

conflicts.statement: What derails an implementation: expert-1 locates the problem in scope definition and the vendor/partner ecosystem's understanding of effort, while expert-2 and expert-3 locate it in data migration and user behaviour, with the platform explicitly not the issue.

positions.gist: Blames a fuzzy definition of done, heavy customization and misalignment between ServiceNow and its partners on realistic timelines.

citation.quote: I think there’s misalignment between ServiceNow and the partner ecosystem on how long things really take.

positions.gist: Says the platform was not the challenge at all; adoption behaviour was, and go-live took ten weeks.

citation.quote: Like I said, about ten weeks from contract to go-live.

positions.gist: Names data migration out of the legacy tool and end-user change management as the two biggest challenges, not scope or partner misalignment.

citation.quote: The biggest challenge was data migration - pulling asset and ticket history out of the legacy ManageEngine tool.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-1 ran a heavily customized, partner-led enterprise programme across 2,000 sites; the others ran smaller, largely in-house configurations where scope was easier to bound.

outliers.gist: Ten weeks contract-to-live with a one-day identity integration - an order of magnitude faster than the others, and the only one reporting no significant platform-side difficulty.

citation.quote: Azure AD sync for user provisioning was straightforward, native integration, took maybe a day to configure.

notable: The three timelines sit at roughly ten weeks, seven months, and nine to twelve months - and only expert-2 reports beating his own expectation ('faster than I expected going in'), while expert-1 overran his by about a quarter.

expert-3 is the only one who used marketplace apps as the default integration route (Azure AD, Slack, monitoring tools), reserving custom scripting for a narrow set of Intune fields - a different posture from expert-1's middle-layer build.
expert-1's most transferable warning is about scope rather than technology: 'lacking a clear definition of done—there was so much customization that scope boundaries were fuzzy'.
Only expert-2 raises legacy data migration as a first-order problem, noting the old tool's export tools 'weren't great' and forced manual cleanup and mapping before loading the new CMDB.
expert-1 says no pre-built integration option existed for his needs at the time, which dates his experience and limits comparison with today's connector marketplaces.
gaps: Nobody gives implementation cost or services spend, so the timeline differences cannot be converted into money.
Only expert-1 discusses working with an external systems integrator, so there is no second account of the partner-ecosystem misalignment he raises.
expert-3 says nothing about data migration from a prior system, so the migration burden is evidenced by one account only.
expert-1 does not describe post-go-live adoption or training effort, so the stabilisation and change-management findings rest on expert-2 and expert-3.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three overran budget, but by very different margins (ServiceNow ~2x competitors and +20-30% in soft internal cost; BMC 15%; Freshservice 5%), and all three hit the same surprise: a module they assumed was included turned out to be a separately-priced SKU. Where they diverge is what drove the overrun - internal validation effort for ServiceNow versus integration work or extra seats for the smaller deployments.

canonical_quote.quote: If I put BMC at roughly sixty dollars a user per month blended across our license tiers, ServiceNow's quote came in closer to one-sixty for a comparable module set, Ivanti was around seventy, and Freshservice was in the thirty to thirty-five dollar range, but again, with less compliance depth.

agreements.statement: Each ran over budget, and each names an unbudgeted module or SKU discovered after signing rather than a mispriced core licence.

positions.gist: Assumed GRC and parts of change management were in the package; they were priced add-ons.

citation.quote: we thought GRC would be included, but it wasn’t. I recall parts of change management also being an extra cost. So we faced some licensing challenges—what we initially assumed was a full package turned out to have add-ons that increased the price.

positions.gist: AIOps/predictive analytics and the full mobile Digital Workplace were separate SKUs added mid-implementation.

citation.quote: that was a separate SKU we had to add mid-implementation once we realized site staff needed mobile ticket submission

positions.gist: The Project module was an unbudgeted add-on, but calls the pricing transparent overall.

citation.quote: The Project module was an add-on we hadn't originally budgeted for - that came later once we decided we wanted it for infrastructure rollouts. Otherwise, pretty transparent pricing overall, which I appreciated.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow is priced at roughly three to four times the alternatives on a per-user basis, by the independent estimates of the two who quoted it.

positions.gist: BMC ~$60/user/month against a ServiceNow quote near $160 for comparable modules.

citation.quote: ServiceNow's quote came in closer to one-sixty for a comparable module set

positions.gist: Freshservice ~$40/agent/month against a ServiceNow quote north of $150.

citation.quote: We're on a tier that comes out to roughly forty dollars per agent per month. ServiceNow's quote for a comparable scope was north of one-fifty.

agreements.statement: Annual renewal increases have run in the mid single digits and are described as manageable.

positions.gist: Two renewals in at 4-6% per year, manageable.

citation.quote: increases have been in the four to six percent range each year, which has been manageable

positions.gist: Two renewals in at 6-8%, manageable but more than he'd like.

citation.quote: increases have been around 6 to 8 percent each time, which is a bit more than I'd like, but manageable

positions.gist: Puts increases around 3-5%.

citation.quote: Yeah, it was somewhere around 3-5%.

conflicts.statement: Whether the hidden cost of an ITSM programme is licensing or internal labour. Expert-1 says the biggest miss was soft internal cost (20-30%) from business-user testing and validation; expert-2 and expert-3 locate their entire overrun in licensing and scope items and never mention internal effort as a cost driver.

positions.gist: Internal validation effort was the single largest expectation miss, adding 20-30% in soft cost.

citation.quote: the biggest miss was the internal level of effort and commitment—pulling additional resources for testing and validation. I’d say that added another 20-30% in cost. It’s soft cost, but we had to pull those resources away from other tasks.

positions.gist: Attributes the 15% overrun to SAP integration work and extra Digital Workplace licences, not to internal labour.

citation.quote: We came in roughly 15% over our initial budget, mostly because of the SAP integration work I mentioned, plus some additional Digital Workplace licenses we ended up needing that we hadn't originally scoped for all of our site-level staff.

positions.gist: 5% over, driven purely by extra agent seats; no internal-effort cost raised at all.

citation.quote: Pretty close to budget, honestly - maybe 5% over, mostly because we added a few more agent seats than planned once field supervisors wanted access.

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-1 describes a ~$40B, 2,000-site ServiceNow programme with mass business-user validation; the others ran far smaller deployments needing less internal mobilisation.

outliers.gist: The only one to report TCO at roughly double competitors and to treat licence-role structure (read-only, approver, ITIL, admin) as an unexpected cost dimension; also the only one whose overrun is dominated by unbilled internal time rather than vendor charges.

citation.quote: ServiceNow’s implementation total cost of ownership was roughly double compared to its competitors.

notable: Expert-2 and expert-3 independently price ServiceNow at $150-160 per user/month for comparable scope - two separate quoting exercises landing in the same band, which is worth more than either figure alone.
Expert-2 attaches a capability caveat to the cheapest option in his own comparison, noting Freshservice at $30-35 came 'with less compliance depth' - i.e. the price spread is not purely margin.
Expert-1 knew about ServiceNow's role-based licence separation in advance and it 'still caught us off guard', an admission that foreknowledge of the licensing model did not prevent the budget miss.
Both expert-2 and expert-3 are two renewal cycles in, so their escalation figures cover the same maturity window and are directly comparable.
gaps: Expert-1's answers are fragmented ('Can you repeat the question?', bare 'Yes' responses), so several of his TCO points cannot be tied to a specific question - the exact scope of his 20-30% and 3-5% figures is uncertain.
Only expert-1 speaks to per-role licence structure as a cost factor; expert-2 and expert-3 were not asked, so nothing can be said about whether BMC or Freshservice role tiers behave similarly.
Expert-1 gives no absolute per-user price for ServiceNow, only a relative 'double', so his figure cannot be placed on the same scale as the others' dollar quotes.

columns_synthesis.headline: Satisfaction is high and tightly clustered (8-9) but recommendation scores fan out, and each expert's stated weakness mirrors a rival's strength: ServiceNow powerful but heavy and expensive, BMC strong on regulated-industry compliance but thin on partners and AIOps, Freshservice easy and fast but hitting ceilings in automation and reporting. Each supplies a concrete failure story traced to the platform's known limitation.

canonical_quote.quote: I remember a manufacturing outage where people were trying to work through the major incident management process and didn’t know how to do it. They struggled with the ServiceNow flow, and it took 30-45 minutes just to create the ticket when it should be a 1-minute process.

agreements.statement: Each platform's chief weakness is a direct consequence of its positioning: complexity/cost for the enterprise suite, ecosystem thinness for the mid-market incumbent, and capability ceilings for the lightweight tool.

positions.gist: Cost, learning curve and implementation complexity; overkill for smaller teams.

citation.quote: It's expensive, especially for smaller companies. There can be a steep learning curve. Implementations are complex and require more internal resources than expected. For smaller teams, it can be overkill.

positions.gist: Small partner ecosystem, AIOps behind ServiceNow, mobile hidden behind an extra tier.

citation.quote: Smaller partner and integrator ecosystem, so specialized integrations can take longer to source help for. The AIOps and analytics story is behind ServiceNow's.

positions.gist: Automation builder clunky at complexity, price creep, inflexible reporting.

citation.quote: The automation builder getting clunky at complexity, renewal price creep, and I'd say reporting could be more flexible - we've had to export to Excel more than I'd like for certain board-level reports.

agreements.statement: Asked whether their worst incident was a platform limitation or their own circumstances, expert-2 and expert-3 both answer 'a bit of both' and split the blame between an unusual local requirement and something the vendor should have handled better.

positions.gist: Unusual SAP config, but BMC should have flagged the risk in the sales process.

citation.quote: A bit of both. Our SAP configuration is unusual enough that even a bigger partner ecosystem might not have had an off-the-shelf answer, but I do think BMC could have flagged that risk earlier in the sales process instead of us discovering it mid-implementation.

positions.gist: Custom compliance format is unusual, but native reporting simply doesn't flex without a paid add-on.

citation.quote: A bit of both - Freshservice's native reporting is decent for standard use cases, but for a very specific custom compliance format, it just doesn't flex enough without going into their analytics add-on, which we haven't purchased.

conflicts.statement: Whether satisfaction translates into recommendation. Expert-3 recommends more readily than he is satisfied (8 satisfaction, 9 recommend, on fit grounds), while expert-2 recommends less readily than he is satisfied (8 satisfaction, 7 recommend, caveated on the partner ecosystem). Same satisfaction score, opposite direction of travel.

positions.gist: Would recommend only with caveats about the smaller partner ecosystem.

citation.quote: Probably a 7. I'd recommend it with caveats about the partner ecosystem being smaller.

positions.gist: Rates recommendation above satisfaction because of fit to size and use case.

citation.quote: A 9. For our size and use case, it's been a really good fit.

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-3 scopes his recommendation to organisations like his own; expert-2 generalises to any buyer, where the ecosystem gap bites harder.

outliers.gist: The only one rating a platform he no longer uses - 9 out of 10 for ServiceNow while reporting that his organisation dropped it and is now struggling with the asset-management gap that left.

citation.quote: Yes. Yes, we're struggling now. We got rid of ServiceNow, and that left a gap in terms of asset management.

notable: The single highest advocacy score in the column comes from the expert who is no longer on the product, which makes it a judgement on the platform rather than on a live relationship.

Expert-1's failure story is the only one with an operational safety edge: a 30-45 minute delay logging a manufacturing outage that 'should be a 1-minute process', and he attributes the fix to training and partner walkthroughs, not to product change.
Expert-3's failure story is quantified in recurring wasted effort - a SOC 2 audit-trail report rebuilt manually in Excel every quarter.
Expert-2 volunteers that the two-month go-live slip forced dual-system running and confusion over where tickets should be logged - a cost that appears in neither his budget nor his renewal figures.
Expert-1 pushes back on the premise that cost is the main reason buyers leave, arguing scalability, integration and regulatory compliance would drive his own view instead.
gaps: Expert-1 was asked follow-ups the others were not (the 'difficult to switch' framing, the pushback question), so his section covers ground with no comparator.
Neither expert-2 nor expert-3 was asked what would have prevented their failure incident, so expert-1's answer on training and partner walkthroughs stands alone.

Expert-1's ratings are given twice (9 and 9) without clear labelling of which is satisfaction and which is recommendation, so the satisfaction/advocacy gap seen in the other two cannot be tested for him.

columns_synthesis.headline: Perceived lock-in scales with depth of customisation, not with vendor: 7-8 for the heavily-customised ServiceNow estate, 6 for BMC with bespoke CMDB and compliance logic, 4 for the standard Freshservice build. All three anchor against ERP as the 10. Most striking, both expert-2 and expert-3 name ServiceNow as their next platform for the same reason - if switching costs must be absorbed, buy the most headroom.

canonical_quote.quote: Probably ServiceNow at this point, just because if we're going to absorb switching costs anyway, I'd want the platform with the broadest long-term ecosystem and AI roadmap, assuming budget allowed it.

agreements.statement: If forced to switch, the destination is ServiceNow, on identical reasoning: once switching costs are unavoidable, buy maximum long-term headroom.

positions.gist: Would go to ServiceNow for the broadest ecosystem and AI roadmap, budget permitting.

citation.quote: if we're going to absorb switching costs anyway, I'd want the platform with the broadest long-term ecosystem and AI roadmap

positions.gist: Would go to ServiceNow for the most long-term headroom once big enough to justify the cost.

citation.quote: Probably ServiceNow, just because if we're big enough to justify switching costs, I'd want the platform with the most long-term headroom.

agreements.statement: Lock-in is real but sub-ERP; ITSM sits in the middle of the entrenchment scale rather than at the top.

positions.gist: 7-8, explicitly benchmarked below ERP at 10, with $1M-$1.5M and at least a year to move.

citation.quote: it's not as difficult as an ERP system—I'd put ERP at 10, a multi-million-dollar project that takes 2-3 years to switch. This would be around 7-8.

positions.gist: 6, also benchmarked below ERP, with custom CMDB and compliance logic as the sticky parts.

citation.quote: I'd put it around a 6. It's not as entrenched as something like an ERP, but we've built a fair amount of custom CMDB structure and compliance workflow logic that would need to be rebuilt or migrated.

positions.gist: 4, and explicitly not entangled - standard integrations, uncustomised data model.

citation.quote: I'd put it around a 4 out of 10. We're not deeply entangled - the integrations are fairly standard, and our data model isn't overly customized. It'd be a project, but not a nightmare.

agreements.statement: A large price shock is a named switching trigger, though the tolerance band differs sharply.

positions.gist: A 30-50% cost increase, 'where it becomes unbearable', plus significant performance issues.

citation.quote: Also, a 30-50% cost increase—where it becomes unbearable—would be another reason to switch.

positions.gist: 25% or more in a single renewal, or a compliance failure the platform can't support a control for.

citation.quote: A sustained price increase well beyond the four to six percent we've seen, say 25% or more in a single renewal, or a serious compliance failure, like an audit finding that the platform itself couldn't support a required control.

conflicts.statement: What actually triggers a switch. Expert-1 and expert-2 frame triggers as things going wrong - price shock, performance failure, an audit finding. Expert-3 frames his primary trigger as growth: outgrowing the platform's automation and reporting rather than the platform failing.

positions.gist: The main trigger is tripling in size and finding Freshservice can't keep up - a scale event, not a failure.

citation.quote: If we scaled significantly, say tripled in size, I'd want to re-evaluate whether Freshservice's automation and reporting could keep up

positions.gist: Triggers are adverse events: a 25%+ renewal jump or an audit finding against the platform.

citation.quote: or a serious compliance failure, like an audit finding that the platform itself couldn't support a required control

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-3 runs a 450-employee estate on a mid-market tool where outgrowth is a live prospect; expert-2's platform already fits his regulated 2,200-employee scale.

outliers.gist: The only one to price a switch in absolute terms ($1M-$1.5M, at least a year) and the only one who names data portability and reduced implementation time - not features - as what a challenger would have to offer to win him.

citation.quote: if they could port the data from ServiceNow to one of those systems and reduce implementation time, that would be significant

notable: Two of the three would move to the platform the third is switching away from, and neither cites current dissatisfaction - the pull is roadmap and headroom, not a defect in the incumbent.

Expert-2 sets his switching threshold against his observed renewal experience ('well beyond the four to six percent we've seen'), making the trigger a multiple of actual escalation rather than an abstract number.

Expert-1's stated exit trigger of 30-50% sits far above the 3-5% he reports having experienced, and he still left ServiceNow - suggesting the actual departure was driven by something other than the price trigger he names here.
Support quality, not price, is expert-3's second named trigger - the only mention of service degradation as a switching cause.
gaps: Expert-1 is not recorded as naming a destination platform in the same terms as the other two, so the ServiceNow-as-destination agreement rests on only two accounts and cannot be tested against someone already there.
Expert-3 gives no price threshold, so his tolerance cannot be compared with expert-1's 30-50% and expert-2's 25%.
Only expert-1 was asked what makes switching hard in practice (implementation effort, underestimated validation resources); the others describe entrenchment but not the mechanics of a migration.

columns_synthesis.headline: Three deployments of the same core ITSM spine - Incident, Request, Problem, Change, Knowledge - at radically different scale: ~2M tickets across 2,000 sites, ~60,000 across a dozen sites, ~18,000 across one 450-person organisation. The differences are in what sits on top of the spine: HR service delivery and GRC at the largest, an employee front-end portal in the middle, a Project module at the smallest.

canonical_quote.quote: It was a very large implementation—about a $40B company with roughly 2,000 sites. We handled around 2M tickets annually. The modules we used included Incident, Request, Problem, Change, and Knowledge. We had a full Configuration Management Database (CMDB), Asset Management, and Major Incident Management.

agreements.statement: All three run the same core module set - Incident, Service Request, Problem, Change - as the foundation of the deployment.

positions.gist: Incident, Request, Problem, Change and Knowledge, plus full CMDB, Asset and Major Incident Management.

citation.quote: The modules we used included Incident, Request, Problem, Change, and Knowledge.

positions.gist: Same core set plus Knowledge and CMDB, with Digital Workplace as the employee front end.

citation.quote: we use Incident, Problem, Change, Service Request Management, Knowledge, and the CMDB

positions.gist: Same core set plus Asset Management and a recently enabled Project module.

citation.quote: We use Incident, Service Request, Change, Problem, Asset Management, and we recently turned on the Project module for some larger infrastructure rollouts.

agreements.statement: Asset management is deployed both at the largest estate and at the smallest, treated as core rather than optional.

positions.gist: Ran full CMDB and Asset Management at Thermo Fisher.

citation.quote: We had a full Configuration Management Database (CMDB), Asset Management, and Major Incident Management.

positions.gist: Asset Management is part of the standard deployed set.

citation.quote: Incident, Service Request, Change, Problem, Asset Management

outliers.gist: Describes a past employer's estate rather than a current one, and is the only one extending the platform beyond IT into HR service delivery and GRC - at a ticket volume roughly 30x the next largest here.

citation.quote: We also used HR—many HR service requests ran through ServiceNow. And we started implementing GRC as another module.

notable: Ticket volume per employee is far more even than headline volume suggests: roughly 27 per employee at expert-2's 2,200-person organisation and 40 at expert-3's 450, so the scale gap is largely a headcount and site-count gap.
Expert-2 has the AIOps suite deployed-but-not-enabled and under evaluation, which matches his later complaint that AIOps was a separate SKU.
Expert-3 notes a rotating pool of field contractors submitting via email-to-ticket, the only mention of a non-licensed requester population, which connects to his overrun from added agent seats.
Expert-2 and expert-3 are both fully cloud-hosted; expert-3 notes Freshservice offers no real on-prem option at all.
gaps: Expert-1 is describing a previous employer (Thermo Fisher) and speaks in the past tense, so his module list is historical and not directly comparable to two live deployments.

Only expert-2 mentions an employee-facing front-end portal; the others were not asked about self-service channels, so nothing can be concluded about how end users reach the platform in the other two organisations.
No agent or licensed-user counts are given by any of the three, only employee headcount and ticket volume, which limits comparison with the per-user pricing discussed elsewhere.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three describe the same pattern: a legacy tool (Zendesk, ManageEngine, or nothing at all) that couldn't deliver speed, asset visibility, or evidence, plus an external compliance driver. Expert-1 frames it around SLAs/MTTR and service quality, while expert-2 and expert-3 put audit trail and asset inventory gaps first.

canonical_quote.quote: Honestly, it was chaos. Nothing was tracked, nothing had an SLA, and when we started scaling up project development, leadership wanted actual metrics

agreements.statement: Lack of a reliable asset/equipment inventory was a named driver in all three accounts.

positions.gist: Centralized management of all IT assets was one of the stated drivers.

citation.quote: We also needed centralized management of all IT assets.

positions.gist: No real CMDB meant no trustworthy inventory of lab or IT hardware.

citation.quote: it didn't have a real CMDB, so we had no reliable asset inventory for our lab equipment or IT hardware

positions.gist: Leadership wanted device deployment counts as a metric.

citation.quote: how many devices we have deployed in the field, that kind of thing

agreements.statement: An external regulatory or audit regime (GxP/Quality in one case, SOC 2 in another) pushed change-control and audit-trail requirements onto the IT tooling decision.

positions.gist: Quality and Regulatory pressed for audit trails on changes touching GxP processes.

citation.quote: We were also getting pressure from Quality and Regulatory to have better audit trails on changes, since a lot of our systems touch GxP-relevant processes.

positions.gist: SOC 2 work for financing partners exposed the absence of any IT change audit trail.

citation.quote: having zero audit trail on IT changes was a real gap

outliers.gist: Alone in framing the decision primarily as a service-performance problem (MTTR, SLAs, routing, user experience) rather than a compliance or evidence problem; compliance appears in expert-1's account only in the following thread.

citation.quote: really it was about improving service levels (SLAs), MTTR, and the user experience from an IT perspective

notable: The three starting points differ in maturity: expert-1 was replacing a functioning-but-slow Zendesk, expert-2 an aging ManageEngine instance, and expert-3 effectively had no system at all - so 'the same drivers' sit on very different baselines.
Expert-3 ties the trigger to a growth event ('when we started scaling up project development') rather than to tool failure per se.
gaps: None of the three was asked to rank or weight the drivers, so it is not possible to tell which one would have carried the decision alone.

columns_synthesis.headline: Expert-2 and expert-3 both describe a bottom-up IT/security project that only became strategic once a compliance argument reached executives; expert-1 describes the same escalation path from site level upward but ends up calling it a genuine digital transformation initiative. Expert-1's cell also carries a separate, unflattering account of a later move away from ServiceNow at a different (smaller) employer.

canonical_quote.quote: It started as an IT-driven project, honestly. I inherited the legacy tool and it was falling apart - outages, tickets getting lost. Once I built the business case around compliance risk, it got elevated

agreements.statement: The initiative originated inside IT and was elevated only after a compliance/risk argument attracted executive sponsorship.

positions.gist: IT-driven until the compliance business case brought in VP of IT and Head of Quality as co-sponsors.

citation.quote: our VP of IT and our Head of Quality co-sponsored it

positions.gist: IT and security-driven until the CFO's office imposed SOC 2.

citation.quote: Mostly IT and security-driven at first. It became more strategic once the SOC 2 requirement came from our CFO's office - that got leadership attention pretty fast.

positions.gist: Escalation ran from site to division to global IT, but expert-1 characterises the endpoint as a strategic digital transformation rather than a scoped IT refresh.

citation.quote: The pain points really started at the site and division levels, and then it became a strategic digital transformation initiative.

conflicts.statement: Whether the platform decision belonged to a broader transformation programme. Expert-1 says it became one; expert-2 explicitly denies that framing for their case.

positions.gist: Local complaints aggregated into a global strategic digital transformation and tool consolidation effort.

citation.quote: So, it started at the site level, grew into a strategic IT initiative, and then was implemented globally.

positions.gist: Grew beyond IT but was deliberately not part of a large transformation programme.

citation.quote: So it became bigger than just an IT refresh, but it wasn't part of some grand ERP-style transformation program.

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-1 describes a large multi-site, multi-division global manufacturer where commonality across sites forced a global programme; expert-2 and expert-3 describe single-site organisations.

outliers.gist: Uniquely reports a reverse move - a predecessor replacing ServiceNow with a simplified Teams/AI custom tool - and openly criticises it as poorly thought through and non-scaling, with lost asset management as the cost.

citation.quote: I don’t think the decision was well thought through and it doesn’t scale, but for the company size at that time, I guess it made sense to simplify the user experience.

notable: Expert-1's account spans two employers: a large regulated manufacturer that consolidated onto ServiceNow (including the GRC module for logging and prioritising risks), and Abzena, which had moved off ServiceNow before expert-1 arrived roughly six months ago.

Expert-1 concedes the anti-ServiceNow rationale at Abzena - simplicity, AI in Teams, easier backend - while judging the outcome a failure; that is an unprompted admission against their own preference.
In both expert-2's and expert-3's accounts the escalating sponsor sits outside IT (Head of Quality; CFO's office), suggesting the compliance owner rather than IT is the one who unlocks budget.
Expert-1 is the only one to name a specific compliance module (GRC) as part of what the platform delivered.
gaps: Expert-2 and expert-3 were not asked about a reverse migration or about downsizing the platform, so expert-1's Abzena experience has nothing to be compared against.
Neither expert-2 nor expert-3 says whether tool consolidation (as distinct from replacement) was an aim.

columns_synthesis.headline: The two who answered describe almost the identical mechanism: a GxP flag set at change creation that routes the change into a Quality review workflow, backed by an audit trail the previous tool could not produce. Expert-1 adds that the platform itself was validated; expert-2 adds electronic signature as a gate before implementation.

canonical_quote.quote: When someone opens a change, they tag whether it's GxP-impacting, and that routes it through Quality for review and electronic signature before it can move to implementation.

agreements.statement: A GxP checkbox/flag on the change record is the trigger that routes the change through Quality - the specific capability the prior tool lacked.

positions.gist: Ticking the GxP box fires routing and change-process workflows Zendesk did not have.

citation.quote: when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have

positions.gist: The GxP tag drives approval routing to Quality; the same flag is the core of the capability gain.

citation.quote: The big one is the change approval workflow tied to GxP flags.

agreements.statement: Quality is the mandatory reviewing party for GxP-impacting IT changes in both organisations.

positions.gist: IT change hands to Quality, which opens its own change for approval, review and testing.

citation.quote: Typically, you have an IT change that then goes to Quality; Quality opens a change, it gets approved and reviewed, you might have to do testing, etc.

positions.gist: The change cannot progress to implementation until Quality reviews and signs.

citation.quote: routes it through Quality for review and electronic signature before it can move to implementation

notable: Expert-1 leads with platform validation as the number one gain - a prerequisite in regulated environments that expert-2 never mentions, though expert-2 stresses the artefact auditors ask for.
Expert-2 gives the sharpest picture of the prior state: 'changes were tracked in email half the time', which is what the audit trail replaces.
Neither describes bespoke development; both present this as configuration of flags and routing, suggesting the capability is largely out of the box.
gaps: Expert-3 was not asked this question. Since expert-3's compliance driver was SOC 2 rather than GxP, the column carries no evidence on what a non-life-sciences audit regime demands of change control.
Neither respondent was asked what the compliance workflow costs in cycle time or user friction, so the trade-off is unrecorded.

columns_synthesis.headline: The shortlists overlap heavily - Jira, Zendesk, Ivanti and Freshservice recur - but the decisive split is over ServiceNow itself: expert-2 and expert-3 both evaluated it, and expert-3 eliminated it early on cost and over-capability while expert-2 kept it in for CMDB and compliance depth. Expert-1's recollection is the least precise.

canonical_quote.quote: We ruled out ServiceNow pretty quickly on cost; it felt like way more platform than we needed at our size.

agreements.statement: Freshservice and Ivanti were both on the evaluation list.

positions.gist: Evaluated Ivanti Neurons for ITSM and Freshservice alongside ServiceNow.

citation.quote: We looked at ServiceNow, Ivanti Neurons for ITSM, and Freshservice.

positions.gist: Same two vendors on the list, with Ivanti included because of prior hands-on experience.

citation.quote: We looked at ServiceNow, Ivanti since I had experience with it, Zendesk, and Freshservice.

agreements.statement: Jira / Jira Service Management was considered by both expert-1 and expert-2, though expert-2 discarded it quickly.

positions.gist: Jira named as one of the biggest alternatives assessed.

citation.quote: We looked at competitors like Jira.

positions.gist: Looked at Jira Service Management but eliminated it early for lacking CMDB and compliance depth.

citation.quote: We also briefly looked at Jira Service Management but ruled it out pretty early - it just didn't have the depth we needed for CMDB and compliance workflows.

conflicts.statement: Whether ServiceNow is proportionate for a mid-sized organisation. Expert-3 rejected it early as oversized and too costly; expert-2 retained it precisely because lighter alternatives lacked the depth needed.

positions.gist: Too much platform for the company's size, and eliminated on cost.

citation.quote: it felt like way more platform than we needed at our size

positions.gist: Kept ServiceNow in contention because lighter tools could not meet CMDB and compliance workflow requirements.

citation.quote: it just didn't have the depth we needed for CMDB and compliance workflows

conflicts.explains_it: Different compliance regimes: expert-2 needs GxP-grade change control and a real CMDB, expert-3 only SOC 2 evidence, so the same depth reads as necessary to one and excess to the other.

outliers.gist: The only one who cannot fully recall the shortlist and the only one to name non-ITSM candidates (Workday's ticket management, BMC) and to re-evaluate the incumbent Zendesk.

citation.quote: The biggest ones were Jira, BMC’s tool, and a few others I’m blanking on.

notable: Expert-1 and expert-3 both had Zendesk in the frame, but from opposite positions - expert-1 was re-examining an incumbent they were leaving, expert-3 was considering it fresh.
Expert-3's inclusion of Ivanti is explicitly driven by the evaluator's own prior experience rather than by requirements - a reminder that shortlists are partly a function of who is running them.
Two different elimination criteria appear: functional depth (expert-2 on Jira Service Management) and cost/fit-to-size (expert-3 on ServiceNow).
gaps: Expert-1's recall is incomplete ('a few others I’m blanking on'), so their shortlist cannot be fully compared with the others'.
None of the three was asked which alternative came second, or what would have changed the outcome, so the strength of each preference is unknown.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three name integration with existing enterprise systems (Workday, SAP, Azure AD/Intune), but the ordering splits by size: the Fortune 500 respondent leads with functionality, UX and scalability and mentions cost only late, while both mid-size respondents put cost first and justify it by their revenue. Each mid-size buyer adds one domain-driven criterion — GxP approval workflows, or asset management for a field workforce.

canonical_quote.quote: Cost was definitely near the top, just given our size - we're not a $40 billion company, we're a few hundred million in revenue.

agreements.statement: Integration with the existing enterprise stack (HR/identity/ERP systems) is a named purchasing criterion for all three.

positions.gist: Names IAM and Workday integration explicitly as an evaluated criterion.

citation.quote: can it integrate with our identity and access management (IAM), with Workday (our HR/HCM system)?

positions.gist: Integration with SAP and Workday sits alongside cost and implementation speed.

citation.quote: integration with our existing systems like SAP and Workday

positions.gist: Integration is scoped to Azure AD and Intune rather than HR/ERP systems.

citation.quote: integration with our existing tools, mainly Azure AD and Intune

agreements.statement: The two mid-size buyers both lead with cost and both tie that ranking directly to company size, and both name implementation speed as the next criterion.

positions.gist: Cost near the top because of revenue scale; implementation speed follows.

citation.quote: Beyond cost, it was implementation speed

positions.gist: Cost number one given size, then speed of implementation.

citation.quote: Cost was number one, no question, given our size. After that, speed of implementation

conflicts.statement: Whether cost belongs at the top of the criteria list. The two mid-size buyers put it first; the enterprise buyer lists total cost of ownership late, behind functionality, UX, scalability, integration and automation.

positions.gist: Leads with functionality; TCO appears near the end of a long list.

citation.quote: The first thing is functionality.

positions.gist: Cost is unambiguously first.

citation.quote: Cost was number one, no question, given our size.

conflicts.explains_it: Company size and budget headroom: a $40B enterprise with 2,000 sites versus organisations in the hundreds of millions of revenue with three-person admin teams.

outliers.gist: The only respondent to raise multi-year scalability, automation/routing, reporting and analytics, and vendor reputation as criteria.

citation.quote: Then how the system scales—can it support growth within 3-5 years?

notable: Admin burden appears only where the team is tiny: expert-2 frames it as a headcount constraint — "since I only have three people supporting the platform."
Each mid-size buyer has one vertical-specific criterion the others do not share: GxP-style approval workflows (expert-2) and asset management across remote sites (expert-3).
gaps: No respondent was asked how these criteria were weighted or scored, so relative importance rests on their own ordering.
Only expert-1 discusses a multi-year growth horizon; the others give no time frame, so it is unclear whether cost-first would survive a longer planning window.

columns_synthesis.headline: Forced into strict rank order, the two mid-size buyers converge almost exactly — cost first, implementation speed third, integration or ease of administration at the bottom — while the enterprise buyer inverts the list, putting integration and scalability above cost. Integration appears in all three top fives but at rank 1, 4 and 5 respectively.

canonical_quote.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems. The second is scalability. Third would be cost, or total cost of ownership.

agreements.statement: Cost / total cost of ownership is the number one ranked criterion for both mid-size buyers, and implementation speed is third for both.

positions.gist: TCO first, implementation speed third.

citation.quote: First would be total cost of ownership.

positions.gist: Cost first, implementation speed third.

citation.quote: First, cost. Second, ease of use. Third, implementation speed.

agreements.statement: Integration makes every respondent's top five, but never higher than fourth for the two mid-size buyers.

positions.gist: Integration ranked first.

citation.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities.

positions.gist: Integration ranked fourth, behind cost, compliance workflows and speed.

citation.quote: Fourth, integration capability.

positions.gist: Integration ranked last of the five, and scoped narrowly to two Microsoft tools.

citation.quote: Fifth, integration with Azure AD and Intune.

conflicts.statement: Where cost sits in a strict ranking. Expert-1 places TCO third behind integration and scalability; both mid-size buyers place it first with no hesitation.

positions.gist: Cost is third; integration and scalability outrank it because of scale.

citation.quote: Third would be cost, or total cost of ownership.

positions.gist: TCO is unambiguously first.

citation.quote: Let me think. First would be total cost of ownership.

positions.gist: Cost is first.

citation.quote: First, cost.

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-1 justifies the inversion by scale — "At that scale, it has to work with your other systems" — whereas the others justify cost-first by their smaller size.

outliers.gist: The only respondent to rank scalability and customization in a top five at all; neither appears in the other two lists.

citation.quote: The second is scalability.

notable: The ranked list is not a straight restatement of the earlier open answer: expert-1 opened the previous thread with functionality first, but functionality does not appear anywhere in the ranked top five.
Expert-2's ranked list reorders rather than drops — compliance workflow support rises to second, above implementation speed and integration.

Ease of use / user experience appears in all three lists but at very different heights: second for expert-3, fourth for expert-1, and only as 'ease of administration for a small team' at fifth for expert-2.
gaps: Nobody was asked whether the ranking was formalised in a scoring model or produced on the spot in the interview, so the precision of the ordering is unverified.
No respondent was asked what fell just outside the top five, so the cut-off is invisible.

columns_synthesis.headline: Because their number one criteria differed, the two respondents who answered describe entirely different proof regimes: expert-1 demanded live demonstration escalating to a hands-on proof of concept for integration, while expert-2 demanded multi-year pricing documentation for cost. The shared principle is that a vendor's claim was not accepted on assertion — but one tested the product and the other tested the quote.

canonical_quote.quote: For example, on integration, we’d ask, can you integrate with Workday? If they said yes in the demo, we’d say, show us.

agreements.statement: Neither accepted the vendor's word on their top criterion; each required documentary or demonstrated evidence before the claim counted.

positions.gist: A demo claim had to be backed by a POC run in the vendor's environment.

citation.quote: Next, a short POC to prove it.

positions.gist: Required multi-year quotes rather than year-one pricing, driven by distrust of later escalation.

citation.quote: We asked all four vendors for detailed multi-year quotes, not just year-one pricing, because we'd heard stories about year-two and year-three increases.

notable: Expert-2 reports vendors responding differently to the same demand: a transparent disclosure of escalation from ServiceNow, a three-year lock from Ivanti, and a comparable multi-year commitment from BMC — the evidence request itself became a differentiator.

Expert-2's account shows a secondary criterion doing the elimination work: "Freshservice was cheapest but their compliance workflow story was thinner, so it dropped down our list fast" — cheapest did not win despite cost being ranked first.
Expert-1 sequences the evidence: demo first, then references, then POC — references are explicitly a fallback rather than the opening ask.
gaps: Expert-3 was not asked this question, so there is no account of what evidence a cost-first buyer with an asset-management emphasis demanded — notable given expert-3 also ranked cost first and would be the natural comparison for expert-2.
Neither respondent was asked whether any vendor failed the evidence test outright, so we only see who passed.

columns_synthesis.headline: In all three cases the winner was not the cheapest option, and the deciding factor was the criterion the buyer had ranked first — scalability and integration for the enterprise, cost-to-capability balance for the mid-size pharma, and asset management plus price fit for the field-workforce buyer. Two independently reject Zendesk as unfit for internal IT.

canonical_quote.quote: They had strong integration and strong scalability. They weren’t as strong on cost—they were a bit higher—but integration, scalability, and customization tipped the scale.

agreements.statement: Zendesk was assessed as fitting customer service or small/mid-market needs rather than internal enterprise IT, and was rejected on capability depth.

positions.gist: Intuitive for customer service and mid-market, but lacking advanced workflow automation and customization.

citation.quote: Zendesk is very intuitive for customer service and fits small to mid-market needs, but it lacks advanced workflow automation and customization.

positions.gist: Built for customer support rather than internal IT, with weak asset management.

citation.quote: Zendesk felt built more for customer support than internal IT - the asset management piece was weak.

agreements.statement: The lowest-priced option lost in each account; price alone did not decide, even for the buyers who ranked cost first.

citation.quote: Jira was very inexpensive but lacked capabilities—around $20-21.

citation.quote: Honestly, it came down to price relative to capability.

citation.quote: Freshservice hit the sweet spot: modern interface, built-in asset management with a discovery agent, and a price point that made sense for us.

agreements.statement: Out-of-the-box fit beat configurable-but-unfinished: vendors lost where their capability required custom configuration to meet the buyer's requirements.

positions.gist: Ivanti was price-competitive but needed custom configuration for GxP; BMC had it baked in.

citation.quote: BMC had more of that baked in already from working with other pharma and med device customers.

positions.gist: Values built-in asset management with a discovery agent, and rejects Ivanti partly for being slow to configure.

citation.quote: built-in asset management with a discovery agent

conflicts.statement: Whether ServiceNow's price premium is defensible. Expert-1 accepted roughly double Zendesk's price and rates ServiceNow's TCO a 6 while still selecting it; expert-2 found it almost triple the BMC quote and says it could not be justified internally.

citation.quote: ServiceNow is very expensive—I'd put it at a 6.

citation.quote: ServiceNow was excellent but it was almost triple our BMC quote for a comparable module set, and for our size, that wasn't defensible internally.

conflicts.explains_it: Scale: expert-1 was buying for ~2M tickets/year at a $40B, 2,000-site company where the incumbent was breaking; expert-2 for a few hundred million in revenue.

conflicts.statement: Assessment of Ivanti. Expert-2 rejects it because its compliance and change-approval workflows fell short of GxP without custom work; expert-3 rejects it on remembered administrative experience from a previous employer rather than functional fit.

positions.gist: Rejects Ivanti on compliance-workflow readiness, not usability.

citation.quote: Ivanti was close in price to BMC, but their compliance and change-approval workflows needed more custom configuration to meet our GxP requirements.

positions.gist: Rejects Ivanti on clunky admin and slow configuration recalled from a prior job.

citation.quote: Ivanti I already knew from my last job, and honestly it wasn't a great memory - clunky admin, slow to configure.

conflicts.explains_it: Different grounds rather than incompatible facts — one judges the compliance module, the other the administrative experience, and from a prior job rather than this evaluation.

outliers.gist: The only respondent to supply numeric vendor scoring, per-seat price benchmarks and a description of the approval chain, and the only one for whom cost was an accepted trade-off rather than a constraint.

citation.quote: For integration, I’d rate ServiceNow 9/10. Zendesk 6/10. Jira 7/10. BMC 7/10.

notable: Expert-1's own scoring undercuts the choice on two of the five ranked criteria: ServiceNow scores 7 on user experience and 6 on TCO, below Jira (8 and 9) and Zendesk (8 and 7) — the win rests on integration (9) and customization (9).

Expert-1 gives concrete magnitudes: ~2M tickets per year, a move from ~$20B to ~$30B revenue, 10-50K added users, and a $100 per user/month ServiceNow baseline against $50-55 for Zendesk and $20-21 for Jira.
Expert-1 is explicit that finance was not the decision-maker — the business case went to finance "mainly to confirm budget alignment," with real influence at director, senior director and VP level.
Expert-3's rejection of Ivanti is the only decision input in this column sourced from a previous employer rather than from the evaluation itself.
Regulatory requirement surfaces in two accounts as a hard gate rather than a preference: GMP/GxP in expert-1's business case and GxP compliance readiness as expert-2's deciding factor.
gaps: Only expert-1 was taken through the extended follow-ups on pricing benchmarks, per-criterion vendor scoring, business case and approval chain; expert-2 and expert-3 give a single paragraph each, so the comparison of decision governance is one-sided.
Neither expert-2 nor expert-3 gives numbers for their alternatives beyond 'almost triple', so the cost gaps they describe cannot be compared with expert-1's figures.
No respondent was asked whether the decision held up in hindsight, so nothing here tests the stated rationale against outcomes.

columns_synthesis.headline: Both raters put ServiceNow at the top on integration (9), and both mark Ivanti down as the laggard among the vendors they share — but they diverge sharply on Freshservice, which expert-2 scores a 6 and expert-3 an 8 based on hands-on Azure AD experience.

agreements.statement: Ivanti is the weakest of the enterprise ITSM tools both rated, scoring 6-7.

positions.gist: Ivanti a 7, below ServiceNow and BMC.

citation.quote: Ivanti a 7

conflicts.statement: How well Freshservice integrates: a two-point spread, with expert-2 placing it last of the four he rates and expert-3 placing it second only to ServiceNow.

positions.gist: Freshservice a 6 — bottom of his list.

citation.quote: Freshservice a 6

citation.quote: Zendesk, maybe a 5.

expert-3 flags his ServiceNow score as 'raw capability' rather than experience, and his Ivanti score as 'in my experience' — the same number can rest on very different evidence.
gaps: expert-1 was not asked this question, so there is no third score to break the Freshservice tie or to corroborate the ServiceNow 9.
Neither rater explains what a point on the scale represents, so the scores are not calibrated against each other.

columns_synthesis.headline: Both raters invert the integration ranking on cost: Freshservice is the cheapest at 9 for both, and ServiceNow the most expensive, though expert-3 penalises it harder (4) than expert-2 (5). canonical_quote.quote: TCO - flip it around. Freshservice would be a 9, BMC an 8, Ivanti a 7, and ServiceNow a 5, just given how expensive it gets at scale.

agreements.statement: Freshservice is the best value at a 9, and ServiceNow the worst, with cost scaling badly against organisation size.

positions.gist: Freshservice 9, ServiceNow 5 because of cost at scale.

citation.quote: Freshservice would be a 9, BMC an 8, Ivanti a 7, and ServiceNow a 5, just given how expensive it gets at scale.

citation.quote: Freshservice a 9, Zendesk an 8, Ivanti a 7, ServiceNow a 4 for a company our size.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow's capability is not in dispute; the objection is that its power comes with configuration burden and cost, so it is over-specified for smaller teams.

positions.gist: Rates ServiceNow 9 on raw capability but 6 on ease of use for a team his size, and notes you must build much of it yourself.

citation.quote: ServiceNow is powerful but complex, I'd put it at a 6 for a team our size.

agreements.statement: Ivanti sits mid-pack on cost at a 7 for both.

citation.quote: Ivanti a 7

citation.quote: Ivanti, from my prior experience, maybe a 5.

conflicts.statement: Whether Freshservice is adequate for asset management and IT-specific depth: expert-2 rates it a 4 and calls it built for lighter-weight support, while expert-3 rates it a 7 and calls its discovery agent solid.

positions.gist: Freshservice weakest of the four at 4, suited to lighter-weight IT support.

citation.quote: Freshservice is weaker here, maybe a 4; it's really built more for lighter-weight IT support use cases.

positions.gist: Freshservice a 7 — good enough, with a workable discovery agent.
